en.title: Gamescom: Germany is Europe’s largest video game market
en.description: Packed exhibition halls in Cologne are a given at Gamescom these days. People's leisure habits in Germany have changed markedly over the past ten y...
en.fullContent:
Packed exhibition halls in Cologne are a given at Gamescom these days. People's leisure habits in Germany have changed markedly over the past ten years and become increasingly digital.

Today, 33 percent of respondents in the latest so-called "Leisure Monitor" say they play video games at least once a week. Only smartphone activities and listening to music have seen even stronger growth.

This year's Gamescom, which was expected to attract more than 350,000 visitors, is being held under the slogan "Games whet the appetite for the future." Henna Virkkunen, vice-president of the European Commission responsible for digital technologies, is also coming to Cologne to talk about the European Union's strategy on games. The EU commissioner will meet Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil, Research Minister Dorothee Bar and North Rhine-Westphalia state premier Hendrik Wust.

Today, Frank-Walter Steinmeier will become the first German president ever to visit Gamescom, where he will open the Gamescom congress.

According to the 2026 annual report on Germany's games industry, revenue from games, games hardware and online gaming services in Germany reached around €9.4 billion in 2025. That represents growth of 4 percent compared with the previous year. This makes Germany the largest games market in Europe and the fifth-largest worldwide.

Industry representatives in Germany are correspondingly confident: “As the world’s biggest games event, Gamescom is once again making one thing abundantly clear this year: we need to make far better use of the unique potential of games and their cultural, economic and technological power. It must be Germany’s and Europe’s ambition to play a leading role as a production hub for games,” said Game managing director Felix Falk ahead of the trade fair.

en.title: First Michigan Retro Game Expo draws big turnout in Kalamazoo
en.description: KALAMAZOO, Mich. — Gamers of all ages gathered in Kalamazoo for the Michigan Retro Game Expo on Saturday.
en.fullContent:
KALAMAZOO, Mich. — Gamers of all ages gathered in Kalamazoo for the Michigan Retro Game Expo on Saturday.

The expo, which organizers said is the first retro game convention to be held in Kalamazoo, took place at the Delta Hotels Kalamazoo Conference Center for a one-day event.

Despite this year being the first year of the expo, organizers couldn't have been happier about the turnout.

"It's a great turnout, this is insane. I didn't know what I expected, but it wasn't a line this far out the door. As of last night, we were just over 700 in presales," said Kris Carlson, CEO of Verge and an organizer of the expo.

The expo offered a myriad of offerings for gamers, including a free play room with classic video games, over 70 art and video game vendors, Dungeons and Dragons sessions, tournaments, and more.

Advertised as an all-ages event, the expo also featured a kids' room with activities geared towards kids. A representative from Nintendo was also at the expo.

en.title: Wow: GTA 6's first gameplay has redefined what videogames are capable of
en.description: Grand Theft Auto 6 ‘Extended Look’ shows off the best looking game ever made
en.fullContent:
Grand Theft Auto 6 ‘Extended Look’ shows off the best looking game ever made

You have to feel sorry for anyone else making a videogame right now. The 27 minute long Grand Theft Auto 6 ‘Extended Look’ is now available to watch on YouTube and Rockstar’s website after its Netflix debut and, after 13 years of development and a virtually unlimited budget, frankly, it makes every other videogame ever made look like it was cobbled together with spit and chicken wire.

What's so staggering at first glance is the sheer level of graphical detail. Every environment looks lived in, every interior is authentically cluttered and every character uniquely realistic in a way that is usually reserved for actual evolutionary biology. Vice City, the game’s Miami analogue, is utterly convincing too, whether viewed from the lofty vantage point of a rooftop bar or down at street level.

What the Extended Look really served to do, though, was give us a better sense of the dual playable protagonists Jason and Lucia, and their relationship. This is a proper Bonnie and Clyde love story, so long as you choose to nurture it. The pair’s relationship has to be maintained with small gestures, as small as pressing a button to hold hands, and apparently while it doesn't factor into how effectively you can rob a bank or hold up a gas station, it will shape how the story plays out.

The whole thing appears to be a more grown up and serious take on the fan favourite Grand Theft Auto formula. A bit like Red Dead Redemption 2, characters move with more weight and momentum and there are more ways to interact with the world around you, rather than just sprinting to the next shootout like a man-shaped mobile weapons platform.

Of course it wouldn't be Grand Theft Auto without a bit of auto, and thankfully the cars were well represented. Based on the footage, Lucia appears to be the ‘wheelman’ of the pair and car chases will be as much about hiding in alleyways like Ryan Gosling in Drive, as they are haring through traffic at 100mph.

en.title: Florida becomes first state to block welfare cash for tattoos, vapes and more
en.description: Florida’s new welfare assistance rules barring recipients from using benefits on tattoos, theme-park admission, vapes and more is a model for other...
en.fullContent:
Florida’s new welfare assistance rules barring recipients from using benefits on tattoos, theme-park admission, vapes and more is a model for other states seeking to put 'common sense' guardrails on welfare spending, Trump admin official says.

Florida is becoming the first state to impose sweeping new limits on how welfare cash can be spent, blocking recipients from using cash-assistance benefits loaded onto EBT cards for purchases like tattoos, theme park tickets, video games, vaping products and other items not generally considered "basic needs" under a plan the Trump administration is urging other states to emulate.

Florida’s cash-assistance program, known as Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA), is funded through the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program. It is separate from SNAP, the food-assistance program, though families may receive both types of benefits through separate balances on the same EBT card.

The Department of Health and Human Services' Administration for Children and Families (ACF) determined Florida’s updated TANF plan to be complete Thursday in a letter sent to Gov. Ron DeSantis and obtained by Fox News Digital. The letter praised the Sunshine State governor for putting "common-sense restrictions" on what it calls inappropriate, luxury and non-essential purchases.

A "We Accept (Food Stamps)" sign hangs in the window of a grocery store in Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

en.title: My Son Has Found an Innovative Way to Play an Online Video Game. I’m Worried About What This Says About Him.
en.description: Care and Feeding is Slate’s parenting advice column. Have a question for Care and Feeding? Submit it here.
en.fullContent:
Care and Feeding is Slate’s parenting advice column. Have a question for Care and Feeding? Submit it here.

I have a 14-year-old son, “Kevin.” He’s gotten into this online multiplayer game. He’s not letting it consume his life, he still does well on his school and other activities, but some of his actions within the game have made me both proud of his successes and worried about them at the same time.

The game itself is a kind of a very long scale, vaguely medieval fantasy thing. You found an estate, you get resources from it, you improve your resources by building various things on your estate, and you raise troops. It’s very hard to directly damage someone else’s estate, but you can raid them for resources, and this is apparently very common. You’re frequently engaged in an all-against-all war of cattle, crystal, and grain theft, and shifting alliances of raiding each other seem to be what most of the game is about.

Kevin has created a new model for his own playing strategy, and it seems to be working. Instead of simply raiding other people, he’s offered them the opportunity to become a “client.” Clientage does require ongoing protection payments, but he actually does provide protection. If anyone else raids you or demands tribute, he’ll start attacking whoever is bothering his clients, even if it’s an economic loser to fight against a stronger opponent. And he’s started coordinating the raiding efforts of his client base in order to present united fronts against threats and dogpile on the player he’s selected as the next person to recruit in.

But it is working. He was so excited when he checked his messages after school and he had two people asking to be his clients that he hadn’t even raided them to “convince” them to sign up.

So I’m both proud of his skills—he clearly is engaging with the game strategically—but I’m also worried that he’s independently recreated the logic of the protection racket. Is this something I should be taking steps about?
